# Walking the graph: eight papers {.unnumbered}

[Drafted]{.status .drafted} [graph v0.4 · steps coded from the full text of the [success set](success-set.qmd) · success score v0 · not yet discussed]{.status-line}

- For each paper: where it **starts**, every **step** the authors took with the node and the mode it belongs to, where it **ends**, and its **success profile**.
- **Map.** Rust: the node where the paper enters. Teal: nodes it visits. Grey: nodes it never uses.
- **Strip.** The steps in order. [→]{.walk-key .ar} a step along an edge the graph draws (or a repeat of the same node). [⇢]{.walk-key .ar .jump} a jump the graph reaches only through other nodes.
- **Table.** One row per step: the node, the mode of inquiry the step belongs to, what the authors did, and the page. Read the table against the paper.
- Each node's letter is the first letter of its verb: **N** new capability · **E** explore: establish the phenomenon · **O** observe · **I** infer a latent quantity (estimate) · **Q** question · **H** hypothesize · **S** simulate or derive the expectations · **D** design the test · **F** find or set the conditions · **C** compare · **V** vary and replicate · **X** exclude · **K** keep the claim · **P** protect · **R** refine. The [crosswalk](unit.qmd#the-graph) maps each node to the modes it serves.
- One reader coded each paper, from the text alone. The order is the order of the paper's account, which may not be the order of the work. Full codings: `private/analysis/success-set/`. Slides: [three of these walks](slides/modes-meeting.html).

## Is the graph right? What these eight say

| Test of graph v0.4 | Result on the eight papers |
|:--|:--|
| Every move can be placed on a node | Yes: no coder needed a node outside v0.4 |
| Steps follow edges the graph draws | 24 of 83 steps (29%); the rest are jumps |
| The textbook route Q → H → S → D → F → O → C is walked | Never |
| D, a discriminating test designed before the data | 1 of 8 papers |
| H, stated rival hypotheses | 5 of 8 papers |
| Entry at a node other than Q or H | 7 of 8 papers |

- The node set holds; the edges do not. Most science moves between nodes in ways the graph draws only as long detours.
- The most frequent jumps: **V ⇢ C** in 4 papers; **S ⇢ C** in 4 papers; **C ⇢ P** in 3 papers; **C ⇢ K** in 3 papers; **X ⇢ V** in 2 papers. S ⇢ C is a derivation compared with data already in hand; C ⇢ X and C ⇢ K are verdicts without a control series, which found conditions force.
- **Next tests.** The same coding on the 24 [matched controls](success-set.qmd#against-matched-controls) and on unsuccessful papers. If ordinary and failed papers walk the same routes, the route does not explain success; if they skip different nodes, the graph has found something.
- **Candidate changes for v0.5:** draw S → C and C → X, K as edges; or make the graph two-level, modes as the outer graph and the hypothesis pass as one mode's inner loop. The room decides.

## The success score (v0)

- Four dimensions, each scored from 0 to 1 against comparable work, then combined. No measure here is settled; the score is a scaffold the group replaces piece by piece.

| Dimension | v0 measure | Compared against | Status |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Impact | Citation percentile | All research articles in the same journal, year, and OpenAlex subfield | Measured |
| Breadth (polymathy) | Mean of two ranks: share of citers outside geoscience; share of references outside geoscience | The three matched controls | Measured, coarse |
| Novelty | Rank of CD₅ disruption | The three matched controls | Measured, but CD₅ is a [poor proxy](success-set.qmd#against-matched-controls); to be replaced by the group's rating on the [Novelty Dossier](rubrics.qmd#novelty-dossier-v1) |
| Advance | The group's blinded rating on the [advance profile](rubrics.qmd#scientific-advance-profile-v1), rescaled to 0–1 | Not yet rated | Pending |

- **Macro score.** The geometric mean of the measured dimensions, each floored at 0.05. A geometric mean does not let a high score on one dimension buy back a near-zero on another, which is what "success on all four" means [@oecd2008]. The arithmetic mean is reported beside it as a sensitivity check.
- **What the v0 scores can and cannot say.** The recognized four score high because they were chosen on citations. The designated four have 1 to 25 citers each, so their breadth and novelty ranks are noise. The weak novelty proxy sinks Gräff and Xu.

## Three contrasting walks

### Shapiro et al. (2005): noise becomes a seismometer

- **Start.** A new capability: Green functions recovered from ambient noise, plus the new USArray stations (p. 1615). Enters the graph at **N** (New capability). [@shapiro2005]
- **End.** K, a capability claim: noise correlations carry shallow and middle crustal structure, mapped at 60–100 km resolution (p. 1617).

### Sun and Davis (2026): boreholes feel the megathrust lock

- **Start.** An unsolved problem: offshore secular strain is hard to measure (p. 1), met with borehole observatories installed on drilling expeditions between 1995 and 2010 (p. 8). Enters the graph at **N** (New capability). [@sun2026]
- **End.** K then R: strain rates of 0.097–0.686 ×10⁻⁶/yr and full shallow locking at northern Cascadia (pp. 4, 7–8); Barbados left unmodeled (p. 8).

### Normandeau et al. (2025): the seafloor freezes and thaws

- **Start.** An anomaly between repeat surveys: hundreds of small mounds in July 2023, absent shallower than 25 m in 2021 (p. 4). Enters the graph at **O** (Observe). [@normandeau2025]
- **End.** K, best explanation by analogy: seasonal freeze–thaw of freshened porewater expands and contracts the seafloor (pp. 1, 9–11).

## Five more walks

### Vine and Matthews (1963): reversed blocks and spreading

- **Start.** An unsolved problem: magnetic anomalies over ridges that no model of uniform magnetization explains (p. 947). Enters the graph at **E** (Explore). [@vine1963]
- **End.** K, best explanation: reversed blocks from spreading under a reversing field, "more plausible" than the alternative (p. 949).

### Rodell et al. (2009): groundwater loss seen from space

- **Start.** An unsolved problem: "there has been no regional assessment of the rate of groundwater depletion" in northwest India (p. 999). Enters the graph at **Q** (Question). [@rodell2009]
- **End.** K, an estimate with an explanation: 4.0 ± 1.0 cm/yr, 109 km³ lost, human use the likely cause (p. 1001); then a comparison with the ministry figure.

## What the walks cannot show

- **Loops are under-counted by design.** A published paper reports the work in the order of its argument: between protocol and paper, 62% of trials changed, added, or dropped a primary outcome [@chan2004]. Our coding followed the paper's order and had no field for a failed attempt, a rerun, or a redesign, so a return and a next step look alike.
- **Loops are at the mode level.** Merging consecutive repeats, the papers return to a node already visited 11 times but to a mode already used 27 times; every paper has at least one return. The [decision tree](decision-tree.qmd) draws the graph at that level.
- **One coder per paper, coding against the graph it tests.** The coder was given the v0.4 nodes, so every step was placed on a node; "no new node needed" is partly an effect of the instruction. No second coder yet, so no agreement figure.
- **Granularity varies.** Vine and Matthews have 17 steps, Normandeau and colleagues and Gräff and colleagues 8. Step counts measure the coder as much as the paper.
- **Labels are not fully consistent.** One Shapiro step is labelled replication where the others use robustness.
- **Supplements unread** for Shapiro, Lam, Sun, and Xu, where methods and robustness checks usually sit.
- **Successes only.** Eight papers chosen for success; no matched control or failure has been coded yet.
- **How to see the loops.** Peer-review files, open discussions, and version histories record changes made during the work. On nine papers with such records, 126 loops were found, and 4 of them (3%) can be read as loops in the final paper ([decision tree, section 6](decision-tree.qmd#what-process-documents-show)). For Gräff and colleagues and for Lam and colleagues, a review sequence can now be coded beside the final-paper sequence.

## For students

- Pick a paper you know. Write its start, its steps as a strip, and its end. For each step, name the node, the mode, and the page.
- Mark the node where the paper entered and the nodes it never needed. Then ask what would have made it a stronger paper, and at which node.
